title: Matrix Effect

references.label: General microbiology/quantitative methods references (ASM, FDA BAM, CLSI)

summary: The influence that components of a sample other than the analyte of interest (the 'matrix' — e.g. blood, soil, food homogenate) have on an assay's signal, which can cause the same true concentration of analyte to read differently depending on what it is dissolved or suspended in.
explanation: A standard curve is typically built using purified analyte in a simple buffer, but real samples contain many other substances — proteins, lipids, pigments, salts — that can interfere with the detection chemistry, either suppressing or enhancing the signal relative to what the same analyte concentration would produce in the clean standard-curve matrix. This means a standard curve validated in one matrix does not automatically transfer to a different sample matrix without checking; the usual way to test for a matrix effect is a spike-and-recovery experiment, where a known amount of analyte is added to the actual sample matrix and the percentage recovered is compared to the expected value.

comparison.example: Spike-and-recovery in the real sample matrix returns close to 100% of the expected added analyte
Spike-and-recovery returns substantially more or less than 100%, indicating the matrix is suppressing or enhancing signal

commonMisconceptions: Assuming a standard curve built in clean buffer will behave identically when applied to a complex real-world sample matrix without verification.
Attributing an unexpected result entirely to biological variability when an unchecked matrix effect may be the actual cause.
